text: MongoDB's documented range-pagination example sorts explicitly: find({_id: {$lt: startValue}}).sort({_id: -1}).limit(nPerPage), carrying the last _id forward. Always add the sort (ORDER BY id in SQL) so each page continues exactly where the last ended.
why: Shows the missing sort step in the teacher's query.

text: PostgreSQL warns that using different LIMIT/OFFSET values to select different subsets of a query result 'will give inconsistent results unless you enforce a predictable result ordering with ORDER BY'. Without a unique order, rows can repeat or vanish between pages.

Keyset ('seek method') pagination works with filters and non-ID sorts. Sort on a deterministic key such as (sale_date, sale_id), filter with a row-values predicate on the last values seen, and back it with an index on the same columns. 'Paging requires a deterministic sort order.'
why: Corrects the 'no complex WHERE clauses' limitation.

text: The real trade-off of keyset pagination is navigation: 'you cannot directly navigate to arbitrary pages', which suits infinite scroll and batch iteration but not page-number UIs.
A normal MongoDB collection 'stores the _id index separately from the documents'. Since MongoDB 5.3, clustered collections can instead store documents in _id order in one WiredTiger file.
why: MongoDB is not physically ordered by _id by default.

text: PostgreSQL tables are heaps: CLUSTER reorders a table by an index once, but 'when the table is subsequently updated, the changes are not clustered'. Keyset pagination is still fast there because of the B-tree index on the key.
why: Shows the speed comes from the index, not physical order.

text: ObjectIds 'are approximately ordered by creation time, but are not perfectly ordered': they have one-second resolution and are generated by clients whose clocks may differ. Sorting by _id is only roughly equivalent to sorting by insert time.
why: Matters when iterating 'the last N minutes' by ID.

text: Twitter's original Snowflake IDs were 41 bits of millisecond time, 10 bits of machine id and 12 bits of sequence. Twitter promised only that they are 'k-sorted ... within a reasonable bound (we're promising 1s...)'.
why: Explains why time-leftmost IDs compare but are not strictly ordered.

text: Elasticsearch's 10,000-hit cap on from/size is the index.max_result_window setting, not a hard-coded constant. Past it, Elastic recommends search_after (with a point in time) and 'no longer recommend[s] using the scroll API for deep pagination'.
why: Corrects 'hard-coded' and names the current cursor API.

text: DynamoDB Query results come in pages of at most 1 MB. You pass the response's LastEvaluatedKey as ExclusiveStartKey in the next request, a cursor rather than an offset. A FilterExpression is applied after the page is read, so a page can be empty yet still return a LastEvaluatedKey.
why: Concrete example of cursor pagination in a hash-partitioned store.

text: In X API v2, older pages come from an opaque cursor: read meta.next_token and send it back as pagination_token (with max_results for page size). The docs advise using since_id for new data instead of paginating repeatedly.
why: Updates the since_id example to the current API.

text: As of Oct 2026 the X API is sold as pay-per-usage with prepaid credits ('No subscriptions-pay only for what you use'), e.g. $0.005 per Post read, capped at 3 million Post reads a month before Enterprise.
why: Resolves the teacher's uncertainty about whether the API is paid.

text: String comparison follows the column's collation ('a set of rules for comparing characters'), and a case-insensitive collation treats 'a' and 'A' as equal. Numeric strings sort lexicographically ('10' before '9'), so pad numeric-looking string IDs to a fixed width.
why: Pitfalls of keyset pagination on string IDs.

text: Martin Fowler observes that 'almost all the successful microservice stories have started with a monolith that got too big and was broken up', and calls the microservice premium 'a drag you should do without' early on.
why: Mainstream backing for the teacher's caution, in milder form.

text: In MySQL InnoDB 'the clustered index ... stores row data' and is normally the primary key. A primary-key range read there really is one B+ tree descent plus a sequential walk of leaf pages, exactly as the teacher describes.
why: Pins down where the teacher's B+ tree picture is exact.
